title: Our AI-assisted chess game reached #1 on IndieDB. Taking the small win.
author: space64-llc
selftext:
Chess Folk reached #1 on IndieDB’s popularity list, and I’m pretty happy about it.

Not “buy a yacht” happy. It’s a visibility milestone, not a sales chart. But when you’ve spent ages working on something, seeing people notice it feels good.

We use AI tools in development and artwork, and we disclose that. I want to defend the programming side in particular, because “AI wrote some code, therefore you didn’t make the game” skips over most of what making a game involves.

Chess Folk is an offline chess game with fictional rivals, tournaments, lessons and local co-op. Strong chess engines already exist. Getting a weaker opponent to make believable mistakes is surprisingly difficult. You want it to overlook something occasionally, not move its queen out of danger and then put it straight back like it forgot the previous turn.

Then there’s the less glamorous stuff. Saving games properly. Tournament progression. Controller navigation. Text that looks fine on your monitor but apparently requires binoculars from someone’s sofa.

AI coding tools are useful for this work. They can help you explore an approach, get an implementation started, investigate a bug or write tests. For a small team, that help matters. A feature that might otherwise sit on the backlog becomes something you can actually try.

Of course, sometimes the generated code looks completely reasonable until you run it. Then you spend an afternoon discovering how creatively something can be wrong.

You still need to understand what you’re shipping. You need to test it, play it and listen when someone says it’s frustrating. “The AI wrote that bit” would be a spectacularly bad response to a bug report.

But I don’t see those limitations as a reason to dismiss the tools. If they save us time on repetitive work, we can spend that time improving the game. That’s a perfectly good reason to use them.

I understand being tired of rushed releases. Criticise the broken features, the awkward controls, the boring gameplay. Those are useful criticisms. Knowing that AI was involved doesn’t tell you whether the developer spent five minutes or five months checking and improving the result.

We’re proud of Chess Folk, including the work that went into it after the first version of anything “worked.” There are still rough edges, and we’re still fixing them.

So we’re taking the small win and getting back to work. AI helped us build the game. Making it worth playing is still our job.
